claims.text: The initial material is a coarse-grained, single-phase CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy with well-equilibrated grain boundaries.
High-strain-rate shear dynamically refines the alloy's grains.
High-strain-rate shear partially amorphizes the grain-boundary or surface region.
The refined or amorphized interfaces are non-equilibrated, high-energy grain-boundary regions.
The disordered, high-energy interfaces have lower cohesive strength than the initial equilibrated boundaries.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion promotes intergranular decohesion and brittle failure.
A ductile-to-brittle transition can occur without impurity segregation or precipitate formation.
Using an ultra-high-vacuum environment minimizes oxidation and exposure to chemically reactive species.
Using an ultra-high-vacuum environment minimizes impurity segregation within the alloy.
At room to moderate temperatures, sufficiently high strain rates activate refinement or amorphization while avoiding significant thermally driven segregation.
High-strain-rate shear will cause a marked decrease in ductility relative to the initial coarse-grained state.
Fracture will occur predominantly along refined or amorphized grain boundaries.
The sheared material will have lower fracture toughness than the initial coarse-grained material.
The unstrained coarse-grained alloy has a favorable strength-ductility combination and conventional ductile fracture behavior.
At higher temperatures, diffusion-driven segregation or equilibrium phase changes may override the mechanically induced boundary-decohesion mechanism.
The calculated average high-angle grain-boundary energy of CoCrFeMnNi at 300 K is approximately 0.87 J/m² and is relatively high for a metal.
At elevated temperature, segregation and nanoclustering of Cr, Ni, and Mn in CoCrFeMnNi can produce decohesion originating at high-angle boundaries and triple junctions.
The cited sliding study found no significant grain-boundary segregation, consistent with negligible sliding-induced temperature increase.
Single-phase FCC high- and medium-entropy alloys containing combinations of Al, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni can undergo a rapid ductility decrease between 400 and 800 °C.

Failure to observe the proposed boundary transformation, or observation of brittleness without a corresponding boundary transformation, would falsify dynamic boundary decohesion as the operative mechanism.
